subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Grammar in Use: Word Classes (Adjectives)
overview: Adjectives describe people, food and objects. In this sub-strand you will find adjectives in a text, use the comparative forms of regular and irregular adjectives, and put adjectives of size and shape in the right order when you talk about meals and kitchen things.

lessons.title: Finding adjectives and regular comparatives
objectives: Pick out adjectives from a short text about food.
Form the comparative and superlative of regular adjectives.
Use than when comparing two things.
lessons.intro: A mango is a noun. Ripe tells us something about that mango. Without adjectives, a shopping list is only a line of names. With them, we can say which fruit is fresh, which pot is large, and which meal is healthier.
lessons.notes:
### What an adjective does
An adjective describes a noun or a pronoun. It often sits just before the noun, or after is, are, was or were.

- a sweet mango (before the noun)
- The mango is sweet. (after is)

Colour, size, shape, taste and how healthy something is can all be adjectives: red, small, round, juicy, fresh, balanced.

Read this text and listen for describing words.

The cook carried a large round tray. On it sat fresh beans, a juicy mango and a small square tin of groundnuts. 'This meal is healthier than tea and sweets,' she said. The hungry pupils agreed that the mango smelled sweet.

The adjectives include large, round, fresh, juicy, small, square, healthier, hungry and sweet. Tray, beans, mango, tin, meal and pupils are nouns.

### Regular comparatives
When we compare, many adjectives take a regular pattern.

- Short adjectives usually add -er and -est: sweet, sweeter, sweetest; fresh, fresher, freshest; small, smaller, smallest.
- An adjective ending in e adds -r and -st: large, larger, largest.
- A short adjective ending in one vowel plus one consonant doubles the consonant: big, bigger, biggest; thin, thinner, thinnest.
- An adjective ending in a consonant plus y changes y to i: healthy, healthier, healthiest; juicy, juicier, juiciest.
- A longer adjective uses more and most: more balanced, most balanced; more delicious, most delicious.

Use than between the two things: This orange is sweeter than that one. Use the when you mean the winner of a whole group: She chose the freshest bunch.

Plump and thin can describe size, but do not aim them at a classmate as a joke. Compare fruit and tins, or speak kindly about health: a more balanced meal, a healthier habit.

keyWords.meaning: a word that describes a noun, such as fresh, round or healthy
the form of an adjective used to compare two things, such as sweeter or more balanced
the form used to compare more than two, such as sweetest or most balanced
an adjective whose comparative follows a usual spelling rule, such as adding -er or using more

examples.problem: Write the comparative and superlative of healthy.
steps: Healthy ends in a consonant plus y.
Change y to i, then add -er or -est.

examples.problem: Complete: This mango is ____ (juicy) than the banana.
steps: Compare two fruits, so use the comparative.
Juicy becomes juicier.
examples.answer: This mango is juicier than the banana.

activity.title: Adjectives in the classroom
materials: Classroom objects such as a book, a tin, a bottle and a piece of fruit if one is available
steps: Read the paragraph aloud. Each learner underlines two adjectives and circles the nouns they describe.
Choose two classroom objects and compare them with a regular adjective: The blue book is smaller than the atlas.
Write three sentences using -er or more, each with the word than.
Check spellings: bigger, healthier, more balanced.

practice.question: Is 'beans' an adjective in 'fresh beans'? What is the adjective?
practice.answer: No. Beans is the noun. Fresh is the adjective.

practice.question: Write the comparative of big and of large.
Make a sentence comparing two fruits with tastier.
practice.answer: The mango is tastier than the lemon. Any correct sentence with tastier than is acceptable.

practice.question: When do we use more instead of -er?
practice.answer: With longer adjectives, such as more delicious or more balanced.

summary: Regular comparatives use -er, -est or more and most, with spelling changes you can learn.
Use than to compare two things.

lessons.title: Irregular adjectives
objectives: Use good, bad, many, much, little and far in their irregular forms.
Choose a regular or an irregular comparative to match the adjective.
Compare foods without unkind comments about people's bodies.
lessons.intro: Good does not become gooder. If you say it, the listener still understands you, but the sentence sounds unfinished. A few common adjectives keep their own forms, and those forms have to be remembered.
lessons.notes:
### The irregular set
These adjectives do not add -er or -est.

- good, better, best
- bad, worse, worst
- many, more, most
- much, more, most
- little, less, least (when little means a small amount)
- far, farther, farthest

Many goes with things you can count: many oranges, more oranges, the most oranges. Much goes with things you do not count one by one: much sugar, more sugar, the most sugar. Little here means a small amount, not a small object. There is less sugar in this tea than in that cup.

Farther is about distance: The market is farther than the school farm.

### Regular beside irregular
Fresh is regular: fresher fruit. Good is irregular: better fruit, not gooder fruit. Bad is irregular: worse, not badder. A long regular adjective still uses more: more careful, not carefuller.

### Sentences about meals
- Beans are better body-building food than sweets.
- Too much sugar is worse for teeth than a piece of fruit.
- This jug has less water than that one.
- Of the three stalls, Grandmother's has the best spinach.
- We should buy more fruit and less oil when the bottle is still half full.

Do not say a person is 'the worst body' or 'less of a friend' because of their size. Compare the food and the habit. If you are worried that someone is ill, tell an adult.

### A quick test you can say aloud
Ask: am I comparing two things, or a whole group? Two things take the middle form: better, worse, more, less, farther. A whole group takes the last form, usually with the: the best, the worst, the most, the least, the farthest.

keyWords.meaning: an adjective whose comparative does not follow the usual -er ending, such as good, better, best
how much of something there is
at or to a greater distance

examples.problem: Complete: This meal is ____ (good) than yesterday's meal.
steps: Good is irregular.
The comparative is better, followed by than.
examples.answer: This meal is better than yesterday's meal.

examples.problem: Choose many or much: We need ____ spinach and ____ tomatoes.
steps: Spinach is treated as a food we do not count leaf by leaf in this sentence, so much or more can fit, but the usual school contrast is much sugar, many tomatoes.
Tomatoes can be counted, so many.
examples.answer: We need more spinach and many tomatoes. Or: much spinach and many tomatoes.

activity.title: Better, worse, more, less
materials: Cards printed with good, bad, many, much, little, far
steps: Turn over a card and say all three forms, for example bad, worse, worst.
With a partner, describe two meal pictures using better, worse, more or less.
Write four sentences. Two must use irregular adjectives and the word than.
Read them aloud and let the group catch any 'gooder' or 'badder'.

practice.question: Write the three forms of bad.
Complete: Of all the drinks, clean water is the ____ (good) choice with a meal.
Which is correct: 'less sugar' or 'fewer sugar'?
practice.answer: less sugar, because sugar is an amount we are not counting as separate items.

summary: Good, bad, many, much, little and far have special forms.
Use better, worse, more, less and farther when you compare two things.

lessons.title: Adjectives of size and shape in order
objectives: Place a size adjective before a shape adjective.
Use a comparative of size or shape without mixing up the order.
Describe a picture of food with adjectives in a clear sentence.
lessons.intro: People say a big round chapati. They do not usually say a round big chapati. Both words describe the chapati, but English has a preferred order, and size comes before shape.
lessons.notes:
### Size, then shape
Size answers how big something is: tiny, small, little, big, large, long, short, tall.
Shape answers what outline it has: round, square, oval, flat, triangular.

When both appear before a noun, say the size first and the shape second.

- a big round chapati
- a small oval egg
- a large square tin
- a long thin bean pod
- a tiny round orange

You do not need a comma between these two adjectives in ordinary sentences.

### Add a comparative carefully
You can compare the size and still keep the shape in the right place.

- This is a bigger round tray than that one.
- She chose the smaller square tin.
- The oval plate is larger than the square plate.

In the last sentence, shape words sit in two noun phrases, and larger is the comparative of size. That is correct because each phrase has its own order.

Avoid a round bigger tray. The ear expects the size word before the shape word.

### Describing a picture
Look at a market picture and build one clear sentence, not a pile of adjectives.

On the left there is a large round basket of mangoes. Beside it is a small square box of tomatoes. The round watermelons are bigger than the oranges. The stall looks fuller than the one across the path.

Fuller is a regular comparative. Bigger is the comparative of big, with the doubled g. They can live in the same description if each sentence stays tidy.

### Make it a habit
Before you speak, tap two fingers: first finger for size, second for shape. If you only have one adjective, use it. Do not add an empty word. 'A round orange' is enough when you are not talking about size. Clear description helps someone else find the right tin, fruit or plate.

keyWords.meaning: how big or small something is
the outline of something, such as round, square or oval
the usual sequence of describing words before a noun
shaped like an egg, rounded but longer than a circle

examples.problem: Put the adjectives in order: a (round, large) basket.
steps: Large is size. Round is shape.
Size comes before shape.

examples.problem: Correct: She bought a square smaller tin.
steps: Smaller is the comparative of size.
Square is the shape and should follow the size word.
examples.answer: She bought a smaller square tin.

activity.title: Describe the picture in order
materials: A picture, comic or drawing of a kitchen or market
Slips of paper with size words and shape words
steps: Sort the slips into a size pile and a shape pile.
In pairs, build five phrases: size, then shape, then a noun from the picture.
Write three full sentences. At least one must use a comparative such as bigger, smaller or larger.
If a tablet is available, type your best sentence and read it to the class.

practice.question: Which phrase is in the right order: 'a round big pot' or 'a big round pot'?
Join small and oval with the noun 'egg'.
Rewrite: He carried a round bigger tray.
practice.answer: He carried a bigger round tray.

practice.question: Write a sentence that compares two plates and uses a shape word.
practice.answer: The round plate is larger than the square plate. Any correct sentence with size order and a comparison is acceptable.

summary: Say size before shape: a small square tin.
Comparatives such as bigger still come before the shape word.
Use adjectives to help someone picture the real object.

quiz.question: Which word is an adjective in 'fresh beans'?
The superlative of big is
quiz.explanation: Big doubles the g and adds -est.

quiz.question: Choose the irregular comparative of good.
There is ____ sugar in this tea than in that one.
quiz.explanation: Less is the comparative of little when we mean an amount.

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: This fruit is worser than that one.
This fruit is worse than that one.
This fruit is baddest than that one.
This fruit is badder than that one.
quiz.explanation: The comparative of bad is worse.

quiz.question: Which phrase uses size and shape in the right order?
quiz.explanation: Size comes before shape, and both come before the noun.

quiz.question: Correct the phrase 'a square smaller tin'.
quiz.explanation: The size word smaller comes before the shape word square.

quiz.question: Why do we bother about adjective order?
options: So descriptions are clear and natural
So we can tease people about their size
So we avoid all describing words
quiz.explanation: The right order makes the picture in the sentence easy to follow.

quiz.question: Write a phrase for a tiny egg that is oval.
quiz.explanation: Tiny is the size and oval is the shape.
